## The delivery lifecycle {#delivery-lifecycle}

Between deliveries the opening page advertises no delivery. Scheduling one takes three steps, and resetting after one takes two.

**Scheduling.**

- [ ] Fill the `delivery:` block in `_variables.yml` (date, venue, event, mode, registration URL), set `track: trust-one-day`, and set `active: 'true'`. Render the opening page (`quarto render index.qmd`), and it shows a "Next delivery" callout with a link to the track. Set `active: 'false'` again afterwards.
- [ ] Decide on recording. If you record, record the talk only, announce it at the start of each recorded stretch, and pause it for the hands-on tasks. Nothing in the day depends on the recording either way.
- [ ] Decide which way the day leans. The deck keeps two kinds of optional run on the `d` key: `tools` (five slides in the tools segment of Part 1 and the nine-slide R tutorial of Part 2) and `methods` (the five-slide methods tutorial of Part 3 and the two slides of multiverse background in Part 4). To make a run part of the main flow, list it under `core-runs:` in the YAML of `slides/trust-one-day.qmd` and render the deck again. A run that is not listed stays optional and can still be switched on live.

**Resetting, before the next delivery.**

- [ ] Export the responses Sheet (File → Download → CSV) and keep it as a dated snapshot, for example `cases/trust/data/class_results_2026-11-06.csv`.
- [ ] Clear the rows of earlier deliveries from the Sheet, so that the chart opens almost empty for the next class, but only once no other case is collecting results in it (see the Form below). Do not touch the Form, the Worker or the field schema; only the rows change from one class to the next.

---

## Before the day

### The week before

- [ ] **The workspace repository.** The pages of the case are part of the course site (`CodeMoreh/applied-replication`), but the workspace (`CodeMoreh/replication-lab-trust`) does not exist on GitHub yet, and every address that points at it is a placeholder until it does: the workspace zip on the setup page and the cheatsheet, the workspace address on the tools slide of Part 1, and the links in the README of the workspace. Create the repository, push it, and download the zip once from its public address to confirm that it unzips into `replication-lab-trust-main`.
- [ ] **The class-results Form.** Out of the box, the helpers of the case submit to the results Form that every case shares, the one set up for the EU-frames case. Every label of this case reads `explore: [tag] trust …` or `declared: [tag] trust …`, and the class chart on the [Multiverse](../cases/trust/multiverse.qmd#class-results) page keeps only the rows whose label carries the word `trust` after the tag. That works as it stands. Clear the Sheet of the rows of earlier deliveries before the day (the data rows below the header of the tab "Form Responses 1"; the Form keeps working), because the EU-frames chart reads every row and would draw trust rows as unclassed diamonds. The alternative, which keeps the classes of the cases apart for good, is a Form of its own, about twenty minutes once, following `facilitator/live-results-setup.md`: copy the Form, link a new Sheet, deploy a second Worker, and wire the new codes into the configuration blocks of `R/spec_tools.R` in the workspace and of the browser lab, and into the class chart of the Multiverse page.
- [ ] **The file of Task 3.** The reproduction needs the file that Multi100 gave the analysts, `McLaren_SRD_final_data.csv` (29 MB), which the workspace does not ship because it holds person-level survey data. `fetch_multi100()` downloads it from `https://osf.io/download/yehpm/` into `data_private/` and checks its MD5 sum (`afc3762de082e3249601973a0986fff3`). Download it yourself once from the address, confirm that the sum matches, and fit the model of 6U3LL on your own machine, so that you know the download works from outside the university network.
- [ ] **Joining instructions.** Send the address of the track page, the setup page with the request to run `source("R/check_setup.R")` until it prints OK and then `source("R/spec_tools.R"); fetch_multi100()` at home, while online, the case study as the pre-reading, the help page, and a reminder to bring a laptop and its charger. The download at home is what keeps Task 3 independent of the wifi of the room.
- [ ] **The tab switching.** Click once through the sequence of Parts 3 and 4 (deck → specification menu and decision map → the Multiverse page and back), which is the one sequence that you run live several times in the day.
- [ ] **The room.** Confirm the projector, the power sockets, the wifi for visitors (webR downloads its engine and the 10 MB extract on first load, and Task 3 needs the OSF for anyone who did not download at home) and whether the room has Vevox or a similar response tool. The slides say "type in chat" for the four held answers of the day. In the room, decide in advance what "chat" means, from the options that the cue sheet below sets out.

### The night before

- [ ] Render the pages of the case and of the track page by page; never run a full `quarto render` of the project while pCloud syncs the folder, because it dies on renamed files. Check that the opening page, the track pages, the case pages and the deck are current, and push if the site is published.
- [ ] **The live-results loop.** Submit one test result from the browser lab (`try_spec()`, then `submit_exploration(nickname = "test-row")`), confirm that it reaches the Sheet with `trust` after the tag, press *Run Code* on the class chart of the [Multiverse](../cases/trust/multiverse.qmd#class-results) page and find the test circle. Then delete the test row from the Sheet.
- [ ] **The workspace, as a participant meets it.** Download the zip afresh, unzip it, open the folder in your IDE, run `source("R/check_setup.R")` (every line OK, the last at 0.1753), run `fetch_multi100()`, render the report and check that Task 3 prints *t* = 46.625, then complete the preregistration block with a dummy specification and render again.
- [ ] **The browser lab, cold.** Open the live page of the lab in a private window on a connection like that of the venue, time the load of the R engine and of the tables of the course, and run the setup cell (120,080 respondents, 0.1753), the cell of the stored reproduction of Task 3 (*t* = 46.625) and the exercise of the analogue (0.174 on 72,620 respondents). The lab is a demonstration: it fits nothing and reads every result from tables that the pipeline of the case writes.
- [ ] **The public record.** Confirm that the three addresses of the records slide load without an account: osf.io/3ajr9, osf.io/e48gd and osf.io/9jvbt, and that the components of the five analysts are reachable from the last one, because it is the target of the three-minute search in Part 4.
- [ ] **The fallback zip.** Put the workspace zip on a USB stick, for anyone whose download fails in the room. Whether the file of Task 3 travels on the stick as well is a decision for CM (see the fallbacks below).
- [ ] Prepare the catch-up card (below) as a ready-to-paste text, and charge everything.

### Opening the room

- [ ] Put the address of the course site, the browser lab and the cheatsheet on the screen or the whiteboard as people arrive, with the wifi details.
- [ ] Hand out the green and red sticky notes, or open the response tool, and say what each means: green, working; red, stuck.
- [ ] Keep four tabs ready: the deck, the [decision map](../cases/trust/map.qmd), the [specification menu](../cases/trust/menu.qmd) and the [Multiverse](../cases/trust/multiverse.qmd) page.
- [ ] Ask who has the file of Task 3 in place already (a show of hands, or a green circle in chat), so that you know how many downloads the first break has to absorb.
- [ ] If you record, announce it now and say what is and is not recorded.

## Run sheet – the one-day course

Times in the part tables are relative: 0:00 is the start of that part. The clock below maps them onto the day.

A 09:30 start ends at 17:30. Shorter breaks need the text of the break slides changed as well (`slides/_segments/shared/_break1.qmd`, `_lunch.qmd`, `_break2.qmd`), and those slides are shared by the decks of every case.
:::

| Break | 1:30–2:00 | 11:30–12:00 |

**Four stretches of the deck are optional**, marked on screen and switched in one keystroke: the five tools slides of Part 1, the R tutorial of Part 2 (nine slides), the methods tutorial of Part 3 (five slides) and the multiverse background of Part 4 (two slides). The timings below assume that you walk about half of each. Walking all of them in full costs about fifteen minutes that the day does not have, and skipping them all leaves the hands-on tasks more room than they need.

### Deck controls {#deck-controls}

| Key | What it does |
|---|---|
| space · right arrow · clicker | next slide, always exactly one: the deck is linear, so that no clicker press can skip a part |
| **`d`** | switch between the **extended** and the **lean** deck, live; in lean mode the optional slides are taken out of the deck and every key skips them |
| **`]`** and **`[`** | jump to the next or the previous part |
| **`g`** | jump bar: type a few letters of any slide title and press Enter |

## The held answers {#held-answers}

Four times in the day the class writes an answer, holds it and releases it together: the estimand statement (Part 2), the reproduced *t* (Part 3), the placement (Part 4) and "declared" before the preregistered run (Part 4). Holding the answers keeps each one independent of the others, and releasing them together is what produces the wall of identical values after the reproduction. The slides say "type in chat"; the cue sheet below says what that means in the room.

**The reproduction moment.** Everyone runs the Task 3 chunk in the workspace, which fits the model of 6U3LL to the file that Multi100 gave the analysts. When most of the class has a number: "Type your *t*, hold it … go." The target is ***t* = 46.625** on 72,733 respondents, with a coefficient of 0.191, the value recorded for 6U3LL. lme4 prints the *t* to more decimals; the first three are what count. Multi100 also recorded 72,700 degrees of freedom, which come from lmerTest and leave the *t* unchanged. The usual departures, and what they mean:

- **A *t* near 42, on about 68,000 respondents.** The participant included the unemployment rate (`unemp`), as N8P2J did, and the Swiss respondents drop out, because the file holds no unemployment rate for Switzerland. The model of N8P2J itself, *t* = 42.148 on 68,113 respondents, is the optional extension of the task, so say so and move on.
- **An error that the file cannot be opened.** `fetch_multi100()` returned `FALSE`, because the download failed or the MD5 sum did not match. The participant follows the shared screen, where your copy is in place, and reads the stored reproduction and the analogue in the browser lab, which gives 0.174 on 72,620 respondents. The next slide explains why the two numbers differ, so the participant loses nothing of the argument.
- **A browser-lab participant with 0.174.** That is the right answer for the lab, not a failed reproduction: the lab cannot read the file, because the OSF does not let a page on another website read it.

**The catch-up card**, for the re-entry to Part 3:

> Just back? You have missed nothing that you cannot recover: (1) if Task 2 is unfinished, run the graph chunk as it stands and come back to the wording later; (2) Task 3 is the reproduction – the target is t = 46.625, the code is on the slide and in your report, and it needs the file that `fetch_multi100()` downloads; without it, follow my screen and run the analogue in the browser lab; (3) Task 4 is exploration, so try two specifications and submit one. Put up a red note and I will come to you during Task 4.

## In person and online {#cue-sheet}

The materials are the same in both settings. What changes is how people answer, flag trouble and pair up.

| Beat | In person | Online |
|---|---|---|
| Held answers | the response tool of the room if it has one; otherwise written on a card and held up on "go" | typed in chat, sent on "go" |
| Working or stuck | green and red sticky notes on the laptop lid | a green circle or "STUCK" in chat |
| Rescues | the facilitator circulates | the problem shown on the shared screen |
| The live chart | on the projector, and on the laptops | everyone opens the Multiverse page |
| Form links | on the screen | pasted in chat |
| Breaks | the countdown slide and the time aloud | the countdown slide and "back at :xx" in chat |

---

## The cutting order {#cutting-order}

When time runs short, cut from the optional runs before anything else, so that the time comes out of a tutorial before it comes out of a task.

- **Part 1** – at 0:30, cut the data-availability slide of Miske et al. to one line and the open-research table to one sentence a row. At 0:58, leave the optional tools run switched off.
- **Part 2** – at 0:34, drop selection to one sentence. At 1:04, skip the R tutorial. At 1:22, Task 2 becomes a demonstration, finished over lunch.
- **Part 3** – at 0:50, the methods run stays off. At 1:05, Task 4 shortens to two calls of `try_spec()` and a submission, but everybody still submits.
- **Part 4** – at 0:00, skip the multiverse background. At 0:26, take few clusters and leaving out one country in one sentence each. At 0:54, show the three-minute search on the shared screen instead of setting it.

**Never cut:** the five analysts and their table · the held estimand statement · the controls of the paper on the graph · the reproduction and its held answer · the Task 4 submission · the standard errors with 16 countries · repetition and the causal reading · the preregistration moment.

---

## Fallbacks {#fallbacks}

Each row names the first move, not the only one, and every ladder ends at a point from which the session can carry on.

| Situation | What to do |
|---|---|
| **An installation fails on the day** | The browser lab demonstrates the whole exercise with the numbers that the course pipeline computed with the code of the workspace, the reproduction of Task 3 included, and sends both submissions; the participant follows the tasks there without fitting anything, and the workspace survives for later. |
| **The workspace download fails in the room** | The zip on the USB stick. |
| **The download of Task 3 fails** | The participant follows the reproduction on the shared screen and runs the analogue in the lab (0.174); the argument of the next slide, that the file rather than the model moves the number, does not depend on having fitted it oneself. A second attempt in the next break often succeeds. Whether to carry the file itself on the USB stick is CM's decision: it is public on the OSF, whose component states no licence for it, and it holds person-level ESS data, so the course has chosen to link to it rather than pass copies around. |
| **The OSF is down** | As above, for the whole class: the reproduction becomes a demonstration from your own copy, and every participant reads the stored reproduction and the analogue in the browser lab. Tasks 4 and 5 do not need the OSF. |
| **The browser lab stalls** | The ladder of the [cheatsheet](../cases/trust/cheatsheet.qmd): a hard reload and the cells above run again, then a second browser, then the shared screen, then the by-hand lookup, in which the facilitator reads the five choices off `spec_curve.csv` and submits the row through the Form. Everyone still gets a mark. |
| **The wifi fails** | The workspace runs offline once its packages are installed and the file of Task 3 is in place, so Tasks 1–5 continue; only the submissions wait. Collect the printed results (the tag, the label, `b`, `se`, `t`, `df`, `n`, `r`) and submit them through the Form when the network returns. The browser lab needs the network for its first load. |
| **The live chart fails** (Form, Worker, CORS) | The chart falls back to the committed `cases/trust/data/class_results.csv`, which holds only its header. Pull the Sheet as CSV, keep the rows that carry `trust` after the tag, put them in place of that file, render the Multiverse page locally and share the screen. The static curve and the reference marks at the top of the page are enough for the debrief. Submissions are safe in the Sheet whatever happens to the chart. |
| **A participant has lost their tag** | It is in `.class-tag` at the root of the workspace; in the lab, `report_result(nickname = "their-tag")` reuses it. |

## Expected numbers {#expected-numbers}

- **Task 1.** The last check of `R/check_setup.R`: the reference specification reproduces at 0.1753 points of distrust per point of concern; the lab prints the same, with 120,080 respondents.
- **Task 2.** 120,080 respondents in 16 countries and 60 country-rounds; 110,732 in the sample of the paper. Cronbach's alpha of the three immigration items 0.84. Mean distrust among the respondents of the paper: parliament 5.08, politicians 6.06, legal system 4.45. The correlation of mean concern with mean distrust of parliament across the 16 countries is 0.68; within the countries it runs from 0.17 to 0.38. The graph: `adjustmentSets(dag)` returns `{ background, ideology, pessimism }`, and `isAdjustmentSet(dag, paper_set)` returns `FALSE`, because the far-right vote and the verdict on services are colliders in the starter graph. ## Debrief questions {#debrief}

Choose by what the class chart shows, not by the order below.

1. **The blocks of the curve.** "Who held constant nothing, and who held constant everything that the paper does? Which of the two is the claim as SCORE selected it, and which the claim as the abstract states it?"
2. **The decisions that did nothing.** "Who changed the weights or the rule for unanswered items and found that the estimate barely moved? Why might an analyst still argue about them?"
3. **Justification.** "Whose causal graph settled their choice of controls? Whose graph could have justified two sets equally well?"
4. **The verdict on services.** "Is a harsh verdict on the public services a cause of distrust, a consequence of it, or both? What would you need to know to decide?"
5. **The standard error of 0.00.** "What should a reader of the paper have been told about the uncertainty, and would it have changed anything here?"
6. **Placement.** "Your placement puts you among 192 justifiable alternatives. What does an analyst at the end of the curve owe the reader that an analyst in the middle does not?"
7. **Robustness, replication and cause.** "Every specification and both replications find the association. What would convince you that concern lowers trust, rather than distrust raising concern?"
8. **How preregistration felt.** "Did writing the block before running change how the result felt when it landed? Would you have chosen differently after the exploration?"
